pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that SRO in multi-principal element alloys raises the maximum strength by increasing the stacking fault energy and modifying dislocation behavior.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the insight from CrCoNi and related alloys to CoCrFeNiTi, proposing a direct annealing route to establish SRO in this alloy and correlating that with improved hardness and strength, a condition not previously applied or reported for this composition.

fields.hypothesis: Promoting chemical short-range order (SRO) in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi increases the stacking fault energy and induces antiphase boundary (APB) effects during dislocation glide, thereby impeding dislocation motion and leading to enhanced hardness and strength.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple random solid-solution (RSS) state with favorable plasticity and machinability but low hardness and strength.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled low-temperature anneal (e.g., near 650 K, chosen based on simulation SRO conditions) for sufficient time to induce measurable SRO without causing precipitation.
fields.conditions: Tests at room temperature under uniaxial compression/tension at comparable strain rates to standard mechanical tests; all samples having similar grain size and chemistry.
fields.structural_mediator: Induced local chemical order (SRO) within the matrix that raises the stacking fault energy and promotes formation of diffuse antiphase boundaries during slip.
fields.mechanism: In the absence of SRO, facile, planar dislocation slip predominates, yielding low resistance to dislocation motion. By contrast, increasing SRO (as shown in PMC9645729) elevates the energy barrier for dislocation glide due to increased SFE and APB formation; this retards dislocation motion and increases the solid solution strengthening, hence the hardness and strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated (as-cast or rapidly quenched) RSS samples, annealed samples with enhanced SRO will display a measurable increase in hardness and compressive/tensile strength. The increase is expected to be moderate; the precise numerical improvement is uncertain without experimental quantification.
fields.baseline: The as-cast or rapidly quenched CoCrFeNiTi alloy in a random solid-solution state.
fields.boundary: This effect is effective only if the annealing temperature and time are carefully controlled to induce SRO without triggering any precipitation or grain growth; tests are valid up to ambient temperature and moderate strain rates.
fields.uncertainty: While the qualitative effect is supported by atomistic simulations of SRO effects (PMC9645729::web::000, PMC9645729::web::004, PMC9645729::web::010), the quantitative magnitude of hardness/strength improvement in CoCrFeNiTi is not precisely predictable beforehand.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples with identical grain size and overall composition. One group is subjected to a controlled annealing treatment at ~650 K to induce SRO, and the other group is rapidly quenched to retain the RSS state. Use identical deformation and hardness testing conditions.
measurements: Vickers or nanoindentation hardness measurements
Compressive/tensile strength tests
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or atom probe tomography (APT) to verify the presence and extent of SRO and APB features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistical increase in hardness and strength is observed in the annealed samples compared to the thoroughly quenched samples, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal increased SRO/APB features, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The detailed atomistic simulations that show distinct dislocation patterning and network formation under multiprincipal slip conditions in MPEAs.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces texture engineering as a novel means of tuning dislocation interactions in CoCrFeNiTi, directly linking controlled slip system activation to enhanced mechanical performance—a parameter not previously exploited in this specific alloy system.

fields.hypothesis: Engineering a textured microstructure in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi that promotes activation of multiple slip systems will enhance dislocation interactions (e.g., collision, formation of sessile dislocations), thereby increasing work hardening and overall hardness/strength despite the inherent ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a random texture that predominantly supports planar slip with limited dislocation collisions and interactions.
fields.intervention: Employ directional solidification or a thermomechanical processing route to induce a preferred crystallographic texture that facilitates multiprincipal slip activation (i.e., simultaneous activation of multiple slip systems).
fields.conditions: Conduct tests at room temperature and at standard strain rates, ensuring that the grain size distribution remains similar between textured and randomly oriented samples.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense dislocation network including sessile dislocations such as stair-rod and Hirth partials, arising from enhanced collisions between dislocations on intersecting slip planes.
fields.mechanism: Based on the atomistic simulation results (e.g., PMC9645729::web::007 and PMC9645729::web::009), activation of multiple slip systems (multiprincipal slip) increases the likelihood of dislocation intersections and reactions, forming a robust, entangled network that serves as obstacles to further dislocation motion. This network increases the work-hardening rate and overall hardness, while still retaining favorable plasticity.
fields.predicted_outcome: Textured samples exhibiting multiprincipal slip will show higher hardness and yield strength compared to randomly textured samples, accompanied by a higher density of sessile dislocations detectable via TEM. The improvement should be moderate but significant, with an expected shift in the strain-hardening behavior.
fields.baseline: Conventional CoCrFeNiTi samples with random grain orientations and predominantly single-planar slip behavior.
fields.boundary: Comparisons must be made between samples with similar grain sizes and in the same testing conditions; the effect is expected under ambient temperature and quasi-static loading conditions.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative enhancement is uncertain because the extent of texture-induced slip system activation and subsequent dislocation interaction is sensitive to processing parameters and may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNiTi samples: one with a conventional random texture and one with an engineered texture (via directional solidification or thermomechanical processing) designed to promote multiple slip system activation. Perform tensile/compression tests and analyze dislocation structures using TEM.
measurements: Hardness measurements (e.g., via nanoindentation)
Tensile or compressive testing to obtain yield strength
TEM imaging for dislocation density and network structure analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the textured samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in dislocation density, work hardening, hardness, or yield strength relative to the random-textured counterparts, the hypothesis will be falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observation that dislocation core characteristics (e.g., undissociated versus spread cores) strongly influence the mechanical strength, suggesting that local chemical environments (i.e. order vs. disorder) govern dislocation mobility.
pool.what_is_new: This proposes that even subtle, nanoscale chemical ordering (short-range order) in a solid solution can mimic the strength-enhancing mechanisms of a fully ordered B2 structure, specifically by increasing local barriers to dislocation motion.

fields.hypothesis: Chemical short‐range order (SRO) in the nominally disordered CoCrFeNiTi alloy acts as a nano‐scale obstacle to dislocation motion, thereby increasing hardness and strength without fully developing long-range B2 order.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its fully disordered, simple solid–solution state with low hardness and moderate strength.
fields.intervention: Apply a moderate annealing treatment (at a temperature lower than that required for long-range ordering) designed to enhance chemical SRO clusters.
fields.conditions: Alloy composition: CoCrFeNiTi (equimolar); annealing performed at a temperature modestly elevated (e.g., 500–600 °C) for times sufficient to promote local chemical fluctuations but not complete ordering; tests conducted at room temperature under compression up to 1% strain.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of chemical SRO clusters that act as nano-scale pinning points for dislocations.
fields.mechanism: Even without forming a long-range ordered B2 phase, local atomic clustering (SRO) increases the local resistance to dislocation motion by introducing spatial variations in lattice friction. This enhanced pinning raises the effective Peierls barrier by locally impeding dislocation core spreading, resulting in increased hardness and strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples with enhanced SRO would demonstrate higher yield stresses and harder responses (likely a noticeable increase in hardness on indentation tests) compared to fully disordered as-cast samples, while maintaining relatively good ductility.
fields.baseline: The initial disordered CoCrFeNiTi exhibits lower strength due to easier dislocation motion associated with a well-spread dislocation core.
fields.boundary: Effective as long as the annealing does not progress to a full long-range order or unwanted phase separation; valid below the temperature where complete ordering sets in.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative effect is uncertain; while a trend of increased strength is expected, the precise magnitude depends on the extent and distribution of SRO, which may be variable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one kept in the as-cast disordered state and one subjected to moderate annealing intended to enhance SRO without full ordering. Use diffuse scattering (X-ray or neutron) or atom probe techniques to verify SRO enhancement, then perform mechanical testing (hardness and compression) and dislocation imaging.
measurements: Atom probe or diffuse scattering for SRO characterization
Mechanical tests to measure yield strength and hardness
TEM to visualize dislocation structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If enhanced SRO does not lead to a statistically significant increase in yield stress and hardness relative to the as-cast state, or if induced SRO unexpectedly decreases ductility without a concurrent strength increase, the hypothesis is disproven.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observation that incidental carbon deposition leads to the formation of TiC, which correlates with increased hardness. This hypothesis extends that idea by exploiting the electro-deoxidation's inherent oxygen-vacancy conditions to control nanoprecipitation kinetics through enhanced carbon availability.
pool.what_is_new: Instead of relying on incidental carbon contamination, this approach purposefully modifies the pressing environment to control TiC nanoprecipitation, thereby explicitly linking the unique characteristics of the electro-deoxidization process with a non-conventional mold design to improve mechanical properties.

fields.hypothesis: Enhancing in‐situ nanoprecipitation by deliberately increasing the carbon pickup during vacuum hot pressing can refine TiC nanoprecipitates and thereby increase hardness and strength without significantly sacrificing plasticity.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi processed via oxide electro‐deoxidization and VHPS using a standard graphite mold, yielding an FCC matrix with limited, uncontrolled TiC formation from incidental carbon contamination.
fields.intervention: Replace or line the graphite mold with a specially engineered carbon-rich surface (or add a controlled, sacrificial carbon coating to the powder) to deliberately boost carbon pickup during hot pressing.
fields.conditions: Maintain standard VHPS parameters (e.g., sintering at 1373 K, 35 MPa for 1 h) in an inert atmosphere; process and compare two samples – one with the modified carbon-enhancing mold and one with the conventional mold – at room temperature under tensile and hardness tests.
fields.structural_mediator: A uniformly dispersed population of fine TiC nanoprecipitates embedded in the FCC CoCrFeNiTi matrix.
fields.mechanism: During VHPS, the increased availability of carbon reacts with Ti (which is prone to form carbides due to its large affinity for carbon under oxygen-depleted conditions produced by electro-deoxidization) to promote rapid and controlled nucleation of fine TiC particles. These nanoparticles act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion, enhancing precipitation strengthening. The unique processing route exploits the oxygen-vacancy structure of the electro-deoxidized powders, which facilitates fine-scale carbide nucleation, a nuance not explored in the original study.
fields.predicted_outcome: The modified sample is expected to show a significant (e.g., 15–30% or more) increase in hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline, with only a moderate decrease in ductility due to the additional strengthening effect of finely dispersed TiC.
fields.baseline: As-sintered equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with the standard graphite mold, which shows high plasticity but relatively low hardness and strength due to limited TiC precipitation.
fields.boundary: Excessive carbon pickup may lead to coarse or continuous carbide networks causing embrittlement; thus, the intervention must be optimized to yield a fine and dispersed TiC morphology.
fields.uncertainty: The precise degrees of strengthening depend on the kinetics of TiC formation under these modified conditions, which are not fully quantified in pre-2025 studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples via VHPS: one using the standard graphite mold and the other using a mold with a deliberately enhanced carbon coating. Characterize microstructures with SEM/TEM to quantify TiC particle size and distribution, and perform Vickers hardness and tensile tests.
measurements: TiC nanoprecipitate size distribution and volume fraction (via TEM/SEM)
Vickers hardness values
Yield and ultimate strength from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-enhanced sample does not exhibit a statistically significant (≥15%) increase in hardness and yield/ultimate strength compared to the baseline, or if no refined TiC nanoprecipitates are observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The paper shows that increased residual oxygen leads to the formation of undesirable brittle phases, which impair mechanical performance. This hypothesis leverages that inherent oxygen content but introduces an oxygen-scavenging element to control and refine oxide formation.
pool.what_is_new: Rather than merely striving for lower oxygen content through process improvements, this proposal intentionally incorporates a reactive element (Y) to transform residual oxygen into beneficial, nanoscale oxide strengthening particles, a strategy not explored in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a minor oxygen-scavenging element to form a controlled oxide dispersion can harness residual oxygen to yield nanometric oxides that strengthen the alloy without inducing brittleness.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produced via oxide electro-deoxidization and VHPS that inherently contains moderate residual oxygen leading to undesired brittle oxide or TCP phase formation.
fields.intervention: Add a small amount (e.g., 1–2 at%) of a reactive element such as yttrium (Y) into the starting oxide powder mix, which will preferentially react with residual oxygen during processing and form stable, nanosized Y-containing oxides.
fields.conditions: Process under the same VHPS conditions (sintering at 1373 K, 35 MPa for 1 h), ensuring an inert atmosphere. Compare the standard alloy with the Y-doped alloy at room temperature under tensile and hardness tests.
fields.structural_mediator: A fine, uniform dispersion of Y-containing oxide (e.g., Y2O3 or Y–Ti–O complex) nanoparticles within the FCC matrix.
fields.mechanism: The added Y acts as an oxygen scavenger, reacting with residual oxygen to form stable oxide dispersoids. These nanoscale oxides obstruct dislocation motion through dispersion strengthening while preventing the formation of larger, brittle oxygen-rich TCP phases. Unlike unguided oxygen incorporation that degrades toughness, the controlled dispersion of oxides enhances both strength and hardness without significantly compromising ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Y-doped alloy should exhibit higher hardness and increased yield and ultimate strength (potentially 10–25% above the baseline) compared to the undoped alloy, with improved toughness due to the avoidance of coarse brittle phases.
fields.baseline: Standard as-sintered equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with uncontrolled residual oxygen leading to the formation of inhomogeneous, brittle oxide or TCP phases, lowering overall strength.
fields.boundary: Excessive Y addition could lead to an oversupply of oxide particles, causing excessive grain boundary pinning and potential embrittlement, so the concentration must be kept low.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative strengthening effect is moderately uncertain since it depends on the precise nucleation and growth kinetics of the Y-induced oxides in the electro-deoxidized matrix.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples: one with the standard starting composition and one with 1–2 at% Y added. Process both by VHPS under identical conditions. Characterize the oxide dispersion using TEM and perform mechanical tests.
measurements: Size and distribution of oxide dispersoids (via TEM/EDS)
Vickers hardness values
Tensile test parameters (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., ≥10–15% increase in hardness and strength with maintained or improved ductility) relative to the baseline, or if the expected fine oxide dispersion is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: the observation in PMC7287792 that dendritic microsegregation exists and may contribute to local softening; it extends this by linking local mechanical heterogeneity (verified by nanoindentation) to bulk mechanical properties.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a processing control via rapid solidification to deliberately minimize nano-scale segregation, integrating local mechanical measurements to directly link microstructural homogeneity with overall deformation, hardness, and strength.

fields.hypothesis: Homogenizing local mechanical response by accelerating the cooling rate to reduce nano‐scale mechanical heterogeneity in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produced by conventional laser cladding, exhibiting a dendritic structure with distinct dendrite cores (Cr/Fe-rich) and softer interdendritic regions (Ti/Ni-rich) as seen in PMC7287792::web::009 and PMC7287792::web::010.

top3.label: C1
top3.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that SRO in multi-principal element alloys raises the maximum strength by increasing the stacking fault energy and modifying dislocation behavior.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the insight from CrCoNi and related alloys to CoCrFeNiTi, proposing a direct annealing route to establish SRO in this alloy and correlating that with improved hardness and strength, a condition not previously applied or reported for this composition.

fields.hypothesis: Promoting chemical short-range order (SRO) in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi increases the stacking fault energy and induces antiphase boundary (APB) effects during dislocation glide, thereby impeding dislocation motion and leading to enhanced hardness and strength.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple random solid-solution (RSS) state with favorable plasticity and machinability but low hardness and strength.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled low-temperature anneal (e.g., near 650 K, chosen based on simulation SRO conditions) for sufficient time to induce measurable SRO without causing precipitation.
fields.conditions: Tests at room temperature under uniaxial compression/tension at comparable strain rates to standard mechanical tests; all samples having similar grain size and chemistry.
fields.structural_mediator: Induced local chemical order (SRO) within the matrix that raises the stacking fault energy and promotes formation of diffuse antiphase boundaries during slip.
fields.mechanism: In the absence of SRO, facile, planar dislocation slip predominates, yielding low resistance to dislocation motion. By contrast, increasing SRO (as shown in PMC9645729) elevates the energy barrier for dislocation glide due to increased SFE and APB formation; this retards dislocation motion and increases the solid solution strengthening, hence the hardness and strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated (as-cast or rapidly quenched) RSS samples, annealed samples with enhanced SRO will display a measurable increase in hardness and compressive/tensile strength. The increase is expected to be moderate; the precise numerical improvement is uncertain without experimental quantification.
fields.baseline: The as-cast or rapidly quenched CoCrFeNiTi alloy in a random solid-solution state.
fields.boundary: This effect is effective only if the annealing temperature and time are carefully controlled to induce SRO without triggering any precipitation or grain growth; tests are valid up to ambient temperature and moderate strain rates.
fields.uncertainty: While the qualitative effect is supported by atomistic simulations of SRO effects (PMC9645729::web::000, PMC9645729::web::004, PMC9645729::web::010), the quantitative magnitude of hardness/strength improvement in CoCrFeNiTi is not precisely predictable beforehand.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples with identical grain size and overall composition. One group is subjected to a controlled annealing treatment at ~650 K to induce SRO, and the other group is rapidly quenched to retain the RSS state. Use identical deformation and hardness testing conditions.
measurements: Vickers or nanoindentation hardness measurements
Compressive/tensile strength tests
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or atom probe tomography (APT) to verify the presence and extent of SRO and APB features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistical increase in hardness and strength is observed in the annealed samples compared to the thoroughly quenched samples, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal increased SRO/APB features, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C3
top3.builds_on: The paper’s observation that dislocation core characteristics (e.g., undissociated versus spread cores) strongly influence the mechanical strength, suggesting that local chemical environments (i.e. order vs. disorder) govern dislocation mobility.
top3.what_is_new: This proposes that even subtle, nanoscale chemical ordering (short-range order) in a solid solution can mimic the strength-enhancing mechanisms of a fully ordered B2 structure, specifically by increasing local barriers to dislocation motion.

fields.hypothesis: Chemical short‐range order (SRO) in the nominally disordered CoCrFeNiTi alloy acts as a nano‐scale obstacle to dislocation motion, thereby increasing hardness and strength without fully developing long-range B2 order.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its fully disordered, simple solid–solution state with low hardness and moderate strength.
fields.intervention: Apply a moderate annealing treatment (at a temperature lower than that required for long-range ordering) designed to enhance chemical SRO clusters.
fields.conditions: Alloy composition: CoCrFeNiTi (equimolar); annealing performed at a temperature modestly elevated (e.g., 500–600 °C) for times sufficient to promote local chemical fluctuations but not complete ordering; tests conducted at room temperature under compression up to 1% strain.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of chemical SRO clusters that act as nano-scale pinning points for dislocations.
fields.mechanism: Even without forming a long-range ordered B2 phase, local atomic clustering (SRO) increases the local resistance to dislocation motion by introducing spatial variations in lattice friction. This enhanced pinning raises the effective Peierls barrier by locally impeding dislocation core spreading, resulting in increased hardness and strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples with enhanced SRO would demonstrate higher yield stresses and harder responses (likely a noticeable increase in hardness on indentation tests) compared to fully disordered as-cast samples, while maintaining relatively good ductility.
fields.baseline: The initial disordered CoCrFeNiTi exhibits lower strength due to easier dislocation motion associated with a well-spread dislocation core.
fields.boundary: Effective as long as the annealing does not progress to a full long-range order or unwanted phase separation; valid below the temperature where complete ordering sets in.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative effect is uncertain; while a trend of increased strength is expected, the precise magnitude depends on the extent and distribution of SRO, which may be variable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one kept in the as-cast disordered state and one subjected to moderate annealing intended to enhance SRO without full ordering. Use diffuse scattering (X-ray or neutron) or atom probe techniques to verify SRO enhancement, then perform mechanical testing (hardness and compression) and dislocation imaging.
measurements: Atom probe or diffuse scattering for SRO characterization
Mechanical tests to measure yield strength and hardness
TEM to visualize dislocation structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If enhanced SRO does not lead to a statistically significant increase in yield stress and hardness relative to the as-cast state, or if induced SRO unexpectedly decreases ductility without a concurrent strength increase, the hypothesis is disproven.

top3.label: C12
top3.builds_on: the finding that the equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi HEA is a simple solid solution with moderate mechanical properties (PMC10573807::web::005, PMC10573807::web::007) and on principles of ordering-induced strengthening known from alloy physics.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that the degree of short-range ordering, modifiable by a mild aging treatment, is the key mechanistic factor that governs the balance between ductility and strength in the equiatomic alloy—a factor not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Subtle short‐range ordering (SRO) variations govern the low hardness and strength by facilitating dislocation glide in the simple solid solution. An annealing treatment at a moderate temperature can modify the extent of SRO, thereby locking in local order that increases barriers for dislocation motion.
fields.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produced via mechanical alloying and SPS in a simple solid‐solution state with a mixed FCC/BCC/HCP structure and high homogeneity (as seen in PMC10573807::web::005 and PMC10573807::web::007).
fields.intervention: Subject the as‐SPS alloy to a low‐temperature aging treatment (for example, 400 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere) to promote and ‘freeze’ a higher degree of short‐range ordering.
fields.conditions: Test at room temperature (25 °C) under quasi-static loading (e.g., nanoindentation and compressive tests). The composition remains equimolar CoCrFeNiTi; processing is identical apart from the additional heat treatment.
fields.structural_mediator: An increased volume fraction of short-range ordered clusters distributed in the simple solid solution that act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
fields.mechanism: In complex solid solutions like equimolar CoCrFeNiTi, competing interactions among constituent atoms may lead to only weak or fluctuating SRO during SPS. This subdued SRO results in low lattice friction and permits easy dislocation glide, yielding moderate hardness and strength despite good ductility. A controlled sub-annealing treatment can enhance and stabilize SRO, thereby increasing local barriers to dislocation motion (analogous to ordering hardening in some alloys), which leads to higher hardness and yield strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: The aged samples are expected to show an increase in hardness and compressive yield strength (on the order of a modest 15–30% improvement, pending optimization), with evidence of increased local ordering observable by diffuse scattering in XRD or high-resolution TEM.
fields.baseline: The as-SPS equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy without additional aging, which shows moderate hardness/strength but favorable ductility.
fields.boundary: The aging treatment must be precisely controlled so that the temperature/time is high enough to enhance SRO but low enough to avoid precipitation of secondary brittle phases. Testing is valid for room temperature deformation (25 °C) and quasi-static loading.
fields.uncertainty: The precise degree of SRO and its impact on dislocation pinning in this HEA is not well quantified; improvements are expected but the exact magnitude requires experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi via identical mechanical alloying and SPS. Subject one batch to a post-SPS aging treatment at 400 °C for 1 hour and leave the other as processed. Characterize both batches with high-resolution TEM/XRD (to assess SRO features) and perform nanoindentation and compression tests.
measurements: XRD diffuse scattering or TEM contrast related to ordered clusters
Nanoindentation hardness
Yield strength from compression testing
Strain-to-failure/dactility assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in SRO indicators and no measurable increase in hardness or yield strength compared to the as-SPS baseline, then the hypothesis is refuted.
